Around 1762 it even flowed backwards at times, and **Lake Walen** rose. The plain was flooded again and again.

In the marshes of the Linth plain, **mosquitoes** multiplied. They spread **malaria**, which was then called “intermittent fever”. Many people fell ill, and the fields yielded little. The hardship was great. That is why the **Diet**, the assembly of the members of the Old Confederation, took up the problem from 1783.

From 1807 the Zurich man **Hans Conrad Escher** led the building work. The engineer **Johann Gottfried Tulla** from Baden also helped with the planning. The Linth was led into Lake Walen in a new channel, the **Escher Canal**. There it now deposits its debris. A second channel, the **Linth Canal**, carries the water from Lake Walen into Lake Zurich. After Escher's death in 1823, his descendants received the honorary name **“von der Linth”**.

After the correction, Lake Walen fell by about **5.5 metres**. The marshes dried out, and malaria disappeared. The marshland became fertile **farmland**. The Linth Correction became a model for many later river corrections in Switzerland and Europe. Tulla later led the great correction of the **Upper Rhine**.

After about 200 years, the embankments had become old and weak. That is why the project **“Flood protection Linth 2000”** was planned. From **2008 to 2013** the Escher Canal and the Linth Canal were renovated. The embankments were strengthened and, in some places, the river was given more room. This also created new habitats for animals and plants.

gewusst: The Linth Correction is regarded as one of the first great national community works in Switzerland.
Because the Linth now deposits its debris in Lake Walen, a delta is slowly growing into the lake at the mouth.

teile.einleitung: Bern is the seat of the government and Parliament of Switzerland. Even so, Bern is officially not called the capital but the **Bundesstadt** (federal city). Here you can find out why that is and what makes Bern the federal city.
wichtigste: The Federal Constitution does not set a capital of Switzerland.
Bern is the seat of the Federal Council, Parliament and the federal administration and is therefore called the federal city.
Before 1848 the leadership of the Diet changed every two years between Zurich, Bern and Lucerne.
At the end of 2023 Bern was only the fifth largest city in Switzerland.
After Zurich main station, Bern station is the station with the most passengers.
SBB and Swiss Post have their headquarters in the Wankdorf district of Bern.

abschnitte.text: In the **Federal Constitution** there is not a word about a capital. Switzerland is a federal state in which the cantons carry a lot of weight, and no city was meant to stand above the others. But Bern is the place where the **Federal Council**, **Parliament** and large parts of the **federal administration** work. That is why Bern is called the **federal city**. In everyday life, however, many people still say capital.

Before 1848 Switzerland was a confederation of states. The representatives of the cantons met at the **Diet** (Tagsatzung). After the **Federal Treaty of 1815** the leadership, the so-called **Vorort** (lead canton), changed every two years between Zurich, Bern and Lucerne. Only the new **federal state of 1848** needed a permanent seat for government and Parliament. The choice then fell on Bern.

Bern is not the largest city in the country. At the end of 2023 Bern was in fifth place behind **Zurich**, **Geneva**, **Basel** and **Lausanne**. Famous is the **old town** with its **arcades**. These covered walkways stretch for around six kilometres through the lanes. They are regarded as one of the longest covered shopping promenades in Europe, and the old town belongs to the UNESCO World Heritage.

Many federal offices lie not only in the city of Bern but also in municipalities around it, the **agglomeration**. For example, the **Federal Office of Public Health** (FOPH) has its seat in the Liebefeld district of the municipality of **Köniz**. Companies close to the Confederation are also in Bern: the **SBB** and **Swiss Post** have their headquarters in the well-connected district of **Wankdorf**.

**Bern station** is the second largest station in Switzerland. Here important long-distance lines between east, west and south cross. Since 2010 there has been the association **Hauptstadtregion Schweiz** (Capital Region Switzerland). In it cantons, cities and regions work together. The **Swiss Spatial Concept** names this region alongside the three large metropolitan areas of Zurich, Basel and Geneva-Lausanne.

gewusst: Because the constitution knows no capital, Bern is legally speaking simply the “federal city”.
The arcades of Bern are together around six kilometres long, so in rain you can stroll through the old town almost dry.

teile.einleitung: The old Lötschberg tunnel is a railway tunnel between Kandersteg in the Bernese Oberland and Goppenstein in the Valais. It was opened in 1913. Since 2007 there has also been the Lötschberg Base Tunnel, deeper in the mountain.
wichtigste: The Lötschberg tunnel connects the cantons of Bern and Valais.
The old tunnel runs from Kandersteg to Goppenstein.
It was opened in 1913.
Cars travel through the tunnel on a car shuttle train.
The Lötschberg Base Tunnel of 2007 is about 35 kilometres long.
It begins at Frutigen and ends at Raron in the Valais.

abschnitte.text: The old **Lötschberg tunnel** was opened in **1913**. It is about 14.6 kilometres long. The north portal is in **Kandersteg** in the Bernese Oberland, and the south portal in **Goppenstein** in the Lötschental. The tunnel belongs to the Lötschberg railway, which runs from **Spiez** to **Brig**. It is a pure **railway tunnel**, and there is no road in it.

Anyone who wants to go by car from the Bernese Oberland to the Valais can use the **car shuttle**. In **Kandersteg** you drive your car onto a train. The **car shuttle train** takes the cars through the tunnel to **Goppenstein**. There you drive back onto the road. That is much shorter than a detour over a pass.

Construction began in 1906. In 1908, water and rubble suddenly broke into the tunnel under the **Gastern Valley**, and many workers lost their lives. For this reason the tunnel was replanned and has since made a bend around this spot. Despite the difficulties, the tunnel was finished in 1913. It was an important part of the railway link from Bern over the Simplon to Italy.

Since **2007** there has been the **Lötschberg Base Tunnel**. It lies much deeper in the mountain and is about **35 kilometres** long. Its north portal is at **Frutigen** in the Kander Valley, and the south portal at **Raron** in the Valais. Fast trains from Bern to **Visp** and **Brig** now run through the Base Tunnel. The old tunnel continues to be used for the car shuttle, freight trains and regional trains.

gewusst: With the Lötschberg Base Tunnel, you can get from Bern to Visp in about an hour.
The Lötschberg railway is operated by BLS, whose name stands for Bern-Lötschberg-Simplon.

teile.einleitung: The national border separates Switzerland from its neighbouring countries. It runs over mountains, through lakes and rivers, and is about 2,000 kilometres long in total.
wichtigste: The Swiss national border is about 2,000 km long.
Switzerland borders Germany, France, Italy, Austria and Liechtenstein.
The canton of Schaffhausen lies almost entirely north of the Rhine.
Lucerne is one of the cantons with no border with another country.
Since 2022 the Federal Office for Customs and Border Security has been responsible.
Since 2008, thanks to the Schengen Agreement, there have been no systematic checks on people.
Samnaun is a customs free area.

abschnitte.text: The Swiss national border is **about 2,000 km** long. Switzerland borders five countries: **Germany** in the north, **France** in the west, **Italy** in the south, and **Austria** and **Liechtenstein** in the east. The border often runs along **mountain ridges**, through lakes such as Lake Geneva or Lake Lugano, and along rivers such as the **Rhine**.

Many cantons have a border with another country, others do not. The canton of **Schaffhausen** lies almost entirely **north of the Rhine** and is therefore mostly surrounded by Germany. Cantons in the middle of the country such as **Lucerne**, Bern or Zug have **no border with another country**. Their neighbours are only other Swiss cantons.

Anyone who brings goods across the border must follow the **customs rules**. Since 2022 the **Federal Office for Customs and Border Security** (FOCBS) has been responsible. Switzerland belongs to the **Schengen Agreement**. That is why, since **2008**, there have been no systematic checks on people at the borders. There are still spot checks and checks on goods, because Switzerland is not in the EU customs union.

The village of **Samnaun** in the Grisons is a **customs free area**. There you can shop duty free, for example for petrol, chocolate or perfume. An **exclave** is a part of a state that is **completely surrounded by foreign territory**. One example is **Büsingen on the High Rhine**: the village belongs to Germany but is completely surrounded by Swiss territory. **Campione d'Italia** on Lake Lugano is also an Italian exclave in Switzerland.

gewusst: In Büsingen, which belongs to Germany, people often pay with francs in everyday life.
Switzerland has its longest shared border with Italy.

teile.einleitung: The Gorner Glacier lies in the Monte Rosa massif south-east of Zermatt. Together with its side glaciers it forms one of the largest glacier areas in the Alps.
wichtigste: The Gorner Glacier lies in the Monte Rosa massif near Zermatt.
In 2017 the Gorner Glacier system was the second largest continuous glacier area in the Alps.
In 2013 the Gorner Glacier was around 12 km long.
The Grenz Glacier is the main arm and begins at the Signalkuppe.
It reached its last peak in 1859.
In 2019 the Gorner and Grenz glaciers separated.

abschnitte.text: The **Gorner Glacier** lies in the **Monte Rosa massif** south-east of **Zermatt**. At around 41 km², the **Gorner Glacier system** was the **second largest** continuous glacier area in the Alps in 2017, after the Aletsch Glacier. In 2013 the glacier was around **12 km** long. Its accumulation area reaches up to the summit region above 4,000 m.

The main arm of the system is the **Grenz Glacier**. It begins at the **Signalkuppe**, which is 4,554 m high, and flows north-west along the Lyskamm. On a rocky ridge above the former confluence, at 2,883 m, stands the **Monte Rosa Hut**. It is the starting point for tours up Monte Rosa.

Every spring the **Gornersee** forms where the Grenz and Gorner glaciers meet, held back by the ice. In summer it usually **drains** within a few days. The meltwater reaches Zermatt through streams and forms the **Matter Vispa** there, which flows through the Mattertal to the Rhône.

Until **1859** the glacier advanced and destroyed alpine huts and meadows. Since then it has been retreating. In 1850 the system covered about 66 km², and in 2015 only around 41 km². That is a decline of around **38 per cent**. In **2019** the link between the Gorner and Grenz glaciers even broke off.

gewusst: When the Gornersee bursts out, the flow in the Gornerbach can rise to as much as 150 cubic metres per second.
From the Gornergrat above Zermatt you have a wide view of the glacier and Monte Rosa.

teile.einleitung: The **European Continental Divide** is a long boundary line right across Europe. On one side of it water flows to the Atlantic, the North Sea and the Baltic Sea, on the other to the Mediterranean and the Black Sea. It also runs right across the Swiss Alps.
wichtigste: The main watershed separates the Atlantic, the North Sea and the Baltic Sea from the Mediterranean and the Black Sea.
From the west it enters the Swiss Alps at Mont Pèlerin above Vevey.
The Lukmanier Pass separates the Rhine and the Po, the Albula Pass the Rhine and the Danube.
The Oberalp Pass and the Maloja Pass do not lie on the main watershed.
At the Witenwasserenstock the Rhine, Rhône and Po meet, as do Uri, the Valais and Ticino.
In the 17th century the Canal d’Entreroches was meant to overcome the watershed at the Mormont.

abschnitte.text: A **watershed** separates areas whose water flows in different directions. The **European Continental Divide** is the most important of them. On one side the water flows to the open **Atlantic**, the **North Sea** and the **Baltic Sea**. On the other side it flows to the **Mediterranean** and the **Black Sea**. From the west it enters the Swiss Alps at **Mont Pèlerin** above Vevey and then runs eastwards along the ridges of the Bernese Alps.

Several Alpine passes lie exactly on the main watershed. At the **Lukmanier Pass** the water flows north via the Medelser Rhine to the Rhine, and south through the Blenio Valley to the Ticino and to the **Po**. At the **Albula Pass** the Albula flows via the Hinterrhein to the **Rhine**. On the Engadine side the water flows into the Inn and on to the **Danube**. Both passes thus separate the area of the North Sea from that of the Mediterranean or Black Sea.

Not every watershed is also the main watershed. At the **Oberalp Pass** the water flows on one side into the Vorderrhein, on the other into the Reuss. Both belong to the Rhine area. At the **Maloja Pass** the water flows on one side via the Inn and the Danube into the Black Sea, on the other via the Mera to the Po and into the Adriatic. Both sides lie on the same side of the main watershed.

At the **Witenwasserenstock** there is a special point at 3,025 m above sea level. Here the catchment areas of the **Rhine**, **Rhône** and **Po** meet. At the same time the three cantons of **Uri**, **Valais** and **Ticino** meet here. The point lies about 224 metres east-south-east of the summit.

In the west of Switzerland the main watershed runs very low at the hill of **Mormont** in the canton of Vaud. That is why from **1638** people tried to build the **Canal d’Entreroches** here. It was meant to link **Lake Neuchâtel** with **Lake Geneva**. The canal ran from Yverdon through a cutting in the Mormont as far as the Venoge near Cossonay. The section to Lake Geneva was never built, because it would have needed about 40 more locks and the money ran out.

gewusst: At the Witenwasserenstock a raindrop can flow towards the North Sea, the Mediterranean or the Adriatic, depending on where it lands.
As early as the 17th century people wanted to travel by boat from Lake Neuchâtel to Lake Geneva on the Canal d’Entreroches.

teile.einleitung: On many mountain summits in Switzerland there stands a large cross, the summit cross. It shows that you have reached the highest point.
wichtigste: A summit cross marks the highest point of a mountain.
Many summit crosses are made of wood or metal.
The cross is a symbol from Christianity.
Often a summit book lies by the cross for people to write in.
Many walkers take a summit photo there.
In a thunderstorm a summit cross is dangerous, because lightning can strike it.

abschnitte.text: The **cross** is a symbol of **Christianity**. Centuries ago, people already put up crosses on mountains as a sign of faith and thanks. Today **summit crosses** mainly mark the **highest point** of a mountain. Not every summit has one: some mountains have a cairn instead, a tower of stones.

Many summit crosses are made of **wood** or **metal**. They often have to be carried up laboriously or brought by helicopter. Clubs, mountain guides or village communities often put up a cross and look after it. Wind, snow and sun are hard on the crosses.

By the cross there is often a **summit book** in a box. Climbers and walkers write their name and the date in it. Many take a **summit photo** and enjoy the view. Among mountaineers, people at the top often greet each other with **“Berg Heil”**.

A summit cross is the highest point for miles around, and often made of metal. In a **thunderstorm**, **lightning** can strike there. So if there is a risk of storms, you should avoid summits and ridges and come down in good time. It is important to check the weather forecast before a trip.

gewusst: Some old summit books are later kept in museums or archives.
Summit crosses are sometimes debated: some people see a religious symbol, others simply a summit marker.

teile.einleitung: The Central Plateau is the hilly landscape between the Jura and the Alps. It stretches from Lake Geneva to Lake Constance. Most of the large cities lie here, and the largest part of the Swiss population lives here.
wichtigste: The Central Plateau lies between the Jura and the Alps.
It stretches from Lake Geneva to Lake Constance.
It makes up about a third of the area of Switzerland.
It mostly lies between 400 and 600 metres above sea level.
The Aare flows right across the Central Plateau.
The soil is fertile, so there are many farms.
The A1 motorway connects Geneva with St Gallen.

abschnitte.text: The **Central Plateau** is one of the three great landscapes of Switzerland, alongside the **Jura** and the **Alps**. It lies between the Jura in the north west and the Alps in the south. It stretches from **Lake Geneva** in the south west to **Lake Constance** in the north east. The Central Plateau makes up about **30 per cent** of the area, that is, roughly a third.

The Central Plateau is not a flat plain but **hilly**. It mostly lies between **400 and 600 m above sea level**, and individual hills such as the Napf are much higher. There are fields, forests, lakes and rivers. The soil is **fertile** and the land is not so steep. That is why grain, potatoes and vegetables grow well here, and there are many **farms**.

On the Central Plateau lie many large cities, for example **Zurich**, **Bern**, **Lausanne**, **Geneva** and **Winterthur**. The largest part of the population lives here, and there are many jobs here in industry, trade and services. Because so many people live in a small space, a lot of building goes on. That is why protecting farmland is an important issue.

The most important river is the **Aare**. It flows through Bern, Solothurn and Aarau and is the longest river that flows entirely within Switzerland. On the Central Plateau there are many lakes, for example Lake Zurich, Lake Neuchâtel and Lake Biel. On the edge lie **Lake Geneva** and Lake Constance. Lake Geneva is the largest lake in which Switzerland has a share.

The most important roads and railway lines in the country run through the Central Plateau. The **A1** motorway connects **Geneva** with **St Gallen** and passes Lausanne, Bern and Zurich. Most InterCity trains also run across the Central Plateau. This way the cities are quickly connected with one another.

gewusst: The ground of the Central Plateau consists largely of molasse, the debris of the young Alps.
Many hills and lakes on the Central Plateau were shaped by the glaciers of the Ice Age.

teile.einleitung: Chur is the main town of the canton of Graubünden. The city lies in the Graubünden Rhine Valley and is often described as the **oldest city in Switzerland**. The Romans already had a base here.
wichtigste: Chur is the main town and largest city of the canton of Graubünden.
Chur lies on the Rhine, and the Plessur flows through the middle of the city.
Chur is often described as the oldest city in Switzerland.
The Romans called the place Curia.
The diocese of Chur is regarded as the oldest diocese north of the Alps.
The Arosa Railway runs through the streets of Chur like a tram.

abschnitte.text: Chur is the largest city and the **main town** of the canton of **Graubünden**. Here the cantonal government and the **Grand Council**, the canton's parliament, work. The city lies in the **Graubünden Rhine Valley**. From there the **Rhine** flows on towards Lake Constance. Right through Chur flows the **Plessur**, which comes from the Schanfigg and flows into the Rhine on the edge of the city.

In the area of Chur people lived over 10,000 years ago. That is why Chur is often described as the **oldest city in Switzerland**. The **Romans** had a base here called **Curia**. From this name Chur later came. The position was favourable, because from here routes led to several Alpine passes.

For many centuries a **bishop** has had his seat in Chur. The **diocese of Chur** is regarded as the oldest diocese north of the Alps. The bishop lives in the **Hof district** above the old town. There also stands the large bishop's church, the **Cathedral of the Assumption of Mary**. It was built in the 12th and 13th centuries.

Chur is an important railway junction of the **Rhaetian Railway**. The **Arosa Railway** starts at the station and at first rolls like a tram right through the streets of the city. Then it runs up to Arosa. Straight from the old town a **cable car** takes visitors up the local mountain **Brambrüesch**. There you can walk and, in winter, ski.

gewusst: From the Roman name Curia the present name Chur came about.
In Chur a train of the Arosa Railway runs right through the streets, just like a tram.

teile.einleitung: Zurich is the most important centre for banks, insurance companies and stock market trading in Switzerland. That is why people speak of Zurich as a financial centre.
wichtigste: The Paradeplatz is regarded as a symbol of the Swiss banking centre.
The Swiss stock exchange SIX Swiss Exchange has its seat in Zurich.
The SMI (Swiss Market Index) covers the 20 largest firms on the stock exchange.
In 2023 UBS took over Credit Suisse.
The Swiss National Bank has seats in Bern and Zurich.
Banks and insurance companies belong to the tertiary sector, the services.

abschnitte.text: On the **Paradeplatz** in the middle of Zurich stand the head offices of large banks. It is therefore regarded as a symbol of the Swiss **banking centre**. Banks keep money safe, grant loans and manage assets. So they offer **services** and belong to the **tertiary sector**.

On a stock exchange, shares and other securities are traded. The most important stock exchange in Switzerland is the **SIX Swiss Exchange** in Zurich. The best-known stock index is called the **SMI**, Swiss Market Index. It covers the **20** largest and most heavily traded firms. If the SMI rises, these shares are worth more on average.

Large insurance companies also have their seats in Zurich. A special kind is **reinsurance**: it insures other insurance companies. In this way an insurance company can also pay very large losses, for example after a storm or earthquake. One of the largest reinsurers in the world has its seat in Zurich.

abschnitte.titel: National Bank and changes in banking
abschnitte.text: The **Swiss National Bank (SNB)** has its seat in **Bern and Zurich**. It makes sure the franc stays stable. In March 2023 the bank **Credit Suisse** got into great difficulties. With the help of the Confederation and the SNB, **UBS** took it over so that the financial system stayed stable.

For a long time Switzerland was known for **banking secrecy**. Banks had to keep information about their customers secret. Other countries criticised that taxes could be evaded in this way. Today Switzerland automatically exchanges information about accounts with many countries.

gewusst: The SIX Swiss Exchange runs not only the stock exchange but also systems for payments in Switzerland.
Switzerland is one of the most important places in the world for managing assets from abroad.

teile.einleitung: The Jungfrau is one of the most famous mountains in Switzerland. Together with the Eiger and Mönch it forms a trio in the Bernese Oberland that can be seen from far away.
wichtigste: The Jungfrau is 4,158 metres high and so is a four-thousander.
The border between the cantons of Bern and Valais runs over its summit.
Eiger, Mönch and Jungfrau stand side by side, and the Jungfrau is the highest of the three.
In 1811 the Meyer brothers from Aarau were the first to reach the summit.
You can see the Jungfrau very well from Interlaken.
In the area of the Jungfrau the Aletsch Glacier begins, the largest glacier in the Alps.

abschnitte.text: The Jungfrau is **4,158 metres** high. Mountains over 4,000 metres are called **four-thousanders**. The border between the cantons of **Bern** and **Valais** runs over its summit. The Jungfrau belongs to the Bernese Alps. Its summit is covered with snow and ice all year round.

In the **Bernese Oberland**, three famous mountains stand side by side: the **Eiger**, the **Mönch** and the **Jungfrau**. They are often called the trio. At 4,158 metres the Jungfrau is the highest of the three, the Mönch is a little lower and the Eiger is the lowest. The mountains can be seen especially well from **Interlaken**. The town lies between Lake Thun and Lake Brienz.

On **3 August 1811**, people stood on the summit for the first time. They were the brothers **Johann Rudolf and Hieronymus Meyer** from Aarau. They were accompanied by two guides from the Valais, Joseph Bortis and Alois Volken. At that time there were no railways into the mountains, and the way over the glaciers was very long and dangerous. Today many climbers go up the Jungfrau every year.

Large glaciers lie around the Jungfrau. This is where the **Aletsch Glacier** begins, the largest glacier in the Alps. It flows south into the Valais. The landscape belongs to the **UNESCO World Heritage Site** Swiss Alps Jungfrau-Aletsch. Like almost all glaciers in the Alps, these glaciers too are getting smaller because of warming.

gewusst: The name “Jungfrau” is an old word for a young, unmarried woman.
The first climbers did not come from the mountains, but from the town of Aarau.

teile.einleitung: Lugano is the largest city in the canton of Ticino and lies on Lake Lugano. The city is known for its viewing mountains, its parks by the lake and its rich cultural life in the Italian language.
wichtigste: Lugano lies on Lake Lugano.
It is the largest city in Ticino.
Funicular railways run up Monte San Salvatore and Monte Brè.
In 1956 the very first Eurovision Song Contest took place in Lugano.
The main square is called Piazza della Riforma.
Since 1996 Lugano has had a university, the USI.
HC Lugano plays ice hockey in the top league.

abschnitte.text: Lugano lies on a bay of **Lake Lugano**. On both sides of the bay stand mountains. In the south rises **Monte San Salvatore**, up which a **funicular railway** runs from Paradiso. In the east lies **Monte Brè**, which also has a funicular railway. From both summits you can see far over the lake and as far as the Alps.

The heart of the old town is the **Piazza della Riforma** with the town hall. There are cafés, concerts and markets there. On the lakeshore lies the **Parco Ciani**, a large city park with old trees and flowers. By the lake also stands the **LAC**, the cultural centre “Lugano Arte e Cultura”. It opened in 2015 and has a concert hall and an art museum.

In **1956** the very first **Eurovision Song Contest** took place in Lugano. Only a few countries took part. Switzerland won, with the singer **Lys Assia**. Today the contest is one of the biggest music shows in the world, and Lugano is its birthplace.

In 1996 the **Università della Svizzera italiana**, or **USI** for short, was founded. It is the only university in Italian speaking Switzerland and has sites in Lugano, Mendrisio and Bellinzona. In sport, Lugano is known for **HC Lugano**. HC stands for Hockey Club, and the team plays in the top Swiss **ice hockey league**.

Around Lugano there are many places to visit. In **Melide**, the park **Swissminiatur** shows well-known Swiss buildings in miniature. By boat you reach villages such as **Morcote** and **Gandria**. Near Lugano, in Montagnola, the writer **Hermann Hesse** lived for a long time.

gewusst: Switzerland won the very first Eurovision Song Contest, and it was even held in Switzerland.
After Zurich and Geneva, Lugano is one of the most important banking centres in Switzerland.

t1g6h434.t: Federal Inventory of Landscapes and Natural Monuments of National Importance

teile.einleitung: The BLN is the Federal Inventory of Landscapes and Natural Monuments of National Importance. It is a list of the most valuable landscapes in Switzerland. The Confederation must treat these areas with special care in carrying out its tasks.
wichtigste: The BLN covers 162 objects.
Together they cover around 19 per cent of the country's area.
The BLN is based on the Federal Act on the Protection of Nature and Cultural Heritage (NHG) of 1966.
The first objects were included in 1977, the last in 1998.
It is binding on federal bodies when they carry out federal tasks.
In 2017 the BLN was revised with precise protection aims.

abschnitte.text: The **BLN** is a list of **162 objects**. It includes large mountain landscapes, lakeshores, bogs and gorges, but also small **natural monuments**. A typical natural monument is an **erratic boulder**, that is, a large stone that a glacier carried a long way. Rock outcrops and other **geotopes** belong to it too. Together the objects cover around **19 per cent** of the country's area.

The BLN is based on Article 5 of the **Act on the Protection of Nature and Cultural Heritage (NHG)**. This act came into force on 1 July **1966**. The first series of BLN objects was determined in **1977**. By **1998** three more series followed. The basis was the private **KLN inventory**, which was drawn up from 1959 to 1963 by Pro Natura, the Heimatschutz (Swiss Heritage Society) and the SAC (Swiss Alpine Club).

The BLN is directly binding on **federal bodies carrying out federal tasks**. This concerns, for example, permits, concessions or subsidies from the Confederation. According to Article 6 NHG, BLN objects should be **preserved intact** or at least spared as much as possible. Exceptions are only possible if there are equal or higher interests of national importance. The BLN has no direct legal effect on property ownership.

In **2017** the Federal Council approved a **revision** of the BLN. Since then every object has a precise description and concrete **protection aims**. This makes it clearer what is especially valuable about a landscape. Some names were also adjusted. Besides the BLN there are further federal inventories, such as the **ISOS** for townscapes and the **IVS** for historic transport routes.

gewusst: BLN objects include well-known landscapes such as the Rhine Falls or the region around the Eiger, Mönch and Jungfrau.
Almost a fifth of Switzerland is thus recorded as especially valuable landscape.

teile.einleitung: Italian is one of the four national languages of Switzerland. It is spoken mainly in the canton of Ticino and in some southern valleys of the Grisons. Many words such as “Ciao” or “Grazie” are also known to children in German-speaking Switzerland.
wichtigste: Italian is one of the four national languages of Switzerland.
It is spoken in Ticino and in southern valleys of the Grisons.
“Grazie” means thank you, “Buongiorno” means good day.
You count “uno, due, tre”, that is, one, two, three.
Italian also appears on Swiss banknotes.
Fewer people speak Romansh than Italian.

abschnitte.text: Switzerland has four **national languages**: German, French, **Italian** and Romansh. The most people speak German, then French, then Italian. The fewest speak **Romansh**. According to the Federal Statistical Office, in 2022 around 8 per cent of the population gave Italian as their main language. The Italian-speaking part is called **Italian-speaking Switzerland**.

Italian is spoken mainly in the canton of **Ticino**. Italian is also at home in southern valleys of the **Grisons**, for example in the **Bregaglia**, the **Poschiavo Valley** and the **Mesolcina** (Misox). The Grisons is the only canton with three official languages: German, Romansh and Italian. Many people in German-speaking Switzerland also speak Italian, often because their families come from Italy.

**“Buongiorno”** is a greeting for the morning and the day. “Buono” means good, “giorno” means day. In the evening you say “Buonasera”. **“Ciao”** is a casual greeting that you say both when arriving and when leaving. So it means hello or bye. If you want to thank someone, you say **“Grazie”**. The reply to that is often “Prego”, meaning “you're welcome”.

In Italian you count like this: **uno, due, tre**, quattro, cinque. So “tre” means three. Then come sei, sette, otto, nove and dieci, that is, six, seven, eight, nine and ten. Some numbers sound similar to French or Romansh. That is because all of these languages descend from the **Latin** of the Romans.

Italian can be found all over Switzerland. On the **banknotes**, all four national languages appear. On many packages in the shop, too, the labelling is in German, French and Italian. Federal laws always exist in Italian as well. And almost every child knows words like pizza, pasta or espresso.

gewusst: The word “Ciao” comes from an old Venetian greeting that meant roughly “I am your servant”.
On the back of many Swiss coins it says “Confoederatio Helvetica”, which is Latin, so that no national language is favoured.

teile.einleitung: Monte San Giorgio is a mountain in southern Ticino on Lake Lugano. It is world famous for its fossils: thousands of very well preserved remains of fish and marine reptiles that lived about 240 million years ago were found here.
wichtigste: Monte San Giorgio is a UNESCO World Heritage Site because of its fossils.
The Swiss part has been a World Heritage Site since 2003, the Italian part since 2010.
The fossils come from the Triassic and are about 240 million years old.
At that time a sea lagoon lay here.
The finds include the ichthyosaur Mixosaurus and the reptile Ticinosuchus.
The fossil museum stands in Meride.

abschnitte.text: **Monte San Giorgio** lies in **southern Ticino** between the two southern arms of **Lake Lugano**, near the border with Italy. It is covered with forest and looks unremarkable from outside. In its rock, however, lies a treasure: in certain layers you find very many **fossils**, that is, petrified remains of animals and plants.

The fossils come from the **Triassic**, more precisely from the middle Triassic. The layers are about **245 to 230 million years** old. At that time a warm **sea lagoon** lay here. On the bottom there was little oxygen. That is why dead animals were not broken down but sank into the mud and stayed very well preserved there. So today you find whole skeletons of **fish** and **marine reptiles**.

One of the best-known finds is **Mixosaurus**, an **ichthyosaur** or fish lizard. Several hundred specimens were found. **Ceresiosaurus** is named after the Italian name of Lake Lugano, **Lago Ceresio**. **Ticinosuchus**, by contrast, was a reptile that lived on land and was related to crocodiles. Its name contains the Latin word **Ticinum** for Ticino. The reptile **Tanystropheus**, with its very long neck, was also found here.

Because of these unique finds, **UNESCO** added the Swiss part of the mountain to the **World Heritage** list in **2003**. In **2010** the Italian part was added. In the village of **Meride** stands the **fossil museum** of Monte San Giorgio. It was converted by the Ticino architect **Mario Botta** and opened in **2012**. There you can see fossils and models of the animals.

gewusst: The fossils from Monte San Giorgio are older than most dinosaur finds.
Many finds from Monte San Giorgio are now in museums in Zurich and Milan.

teile.einleitung: Farmers in Switzerland receive money from the Confederation, so-called **direct payments**. They compensate for services from which everyone benefits: well-kept landscapes, biodiversity and animal welfare. Here you can find out how the system works.
wichtigste: Every year the Confederation pays around 2.8 billion francs in direct payments.
The basis is Article 104 of the Federal Constitution of 1996.
A precondition is the proof of ecological performance (PEP).
As a rule, 7 per cent of the area must be biodiversity promotion areas.
The Federal Office for Agriculture is responsible, and payment is made through the cantons.
There are, for example, RAUS contributions, slope contributions and landscape quality contributions.

abschnitte.text: In the past the state guaranteed farmers fixed **prices** and the **purchase** of their products. That led to **overproduction**, for example to mountains of butter and cheese. Today the Confederation instead pays **direct payments**. They compensate for **services in the public interest**, that is, work done for the community, and do not depend on the quantity produced. These include landscape care and biodiversity.

The basis is **Article 104** of the **Federal Constitution**. The people accepted it in **1996**. It describes the tasks of agriculture, such as the secure supply of food and the care of the cultural landscape. The **Federal Office for Agriculture** (FOAG) is responsible for putting it into practice. The money is paid out through the **cantons**. For years the total has been around **2.8 billion francs** a year.

Direct payments are only given if a farm provides the **proof of ecological performance**, **PEP** for short. This includes a balanced **fertiliser budget**, so no more fertiliser than necessary. A regulated **crop rotation** is also important, so that the same thing does not grow in a field every year. As a rule, **7 per cent** of the agricultural area must be **biodiversity promotion areas**, such as extensive meadows or hedges.

Part of the direct payments promotes **animal welfare**. Farms whose animals are regularly allowed outdoors receive the **RAUS contributions**. RAUS stands for “regelmässiger Auslauf ins Freie”, which means regular access to the outdoors. The animals then go on the pasture or into an outdoor run. In this way the Confederation supports animal-friendly husbandry.

Steep meadows are hard to mow and need a lot of work. That is why mountain farmers receive **slope contributions**. They belong to the **cultural landscape contributions** and are meant to prevent such areas from **becoming overgrown**, that is, growing over with scrub. With agricultural policy 2014 to 2017 the **landscape quality contributions** were added. In regional projects of the cantons they promote, for example, standard fruit orchards or dry-stone walls.

gewusst: RAUS is an abbreviation and means “regelmässiger Auslauf ins Freie”, regular access to the outdoors.
Direct payments are the largest part of the Confederation’s spending on agriculture.

teile.einleitung: A hairpin bend is a very tight bend in which the road almost completely turns back on itself. There are many of them on Swiss pass roads. They help cars and bikes to get over steep mountains.
wichtigste: Seen from above, a hairpin bend looks like a bent hairpin.
It is also called a switchback.
Pass roads have many switchbacks so that they are not too steep.
From above, such a road looks like a zigzag.
In hairpin bends you have to drive slowly and carefully.
Crash barriers or walls protect the edge of the road.

abschnitte.text: A **hairpin** is a thin, bent pin used to hold hair in place. At one end it is almost completely bent back. A **hairpin bend** has the same shape: the road makes an almost complete **U-turn**. Such bends are also called **switchbacks**, because the road almost reverses direction.

A mountain is often very steep. A road going straight up would be far too steep for cars, lorries and bikes. So the road goes up the slope in a **zigzag**. Each switchback makes the route longer, but less steep. From above, such a road looks like a snake or a zigzag. One example is the **Tremola** on the Gotthard.

In a hairpin bend you cannot see far, and the bend is very tight. So you have to drive **slowly and carefully**. At the edge there are often **crash barriers** or walls. They stop vehicles if they go too far out. Cyclists, too, have to brake well going downhill.

Long vehicles such as **PostBuses** or coaches need a lot of room in tight bends. They often have to swing out wide and use the whole width of the road. That is why the PostBus sounds its well-known **three-tone horn** before blind bends. On specially marked **mountain post roads**, PostBuses have right of way.

Roads with many hairpin bends are popular with cyclists. In the **Tour de Suisse**, a cycle race through Switzerland, the professionals often ride over steep passes. In big races abroad, too, mountain roads with many switchbacks are famous.

gewusst: The Stelvio Pass in Italy has 48 numbered switchbacks on one side.
The melody of the PostBus horn comes from an opera by Gioachino Rossini.

teile.einleitung: The Gotthard Pass is one of the most famous Alpine passes in Switzerland. It links the canton of Uri in the north with the canton of Ticino in the south and was already an important route across the Alps in the Middle Ages.
wichtigste: The Gotthard Pass links Uri with Ticino.
The top of the pass is at around 2,100 metres above sea level.
Andermatt lies on the north side and Airolo on the south side.
The Tremola is a winding, cobbled road on the Ticino side.
The Devil's Bridge crosses the Reuss in the Schöllenen Gorge.
The first railway tunnel opened in 1882 and the road tunnel in 1980.
In winter the pass road is closed because of snow.

abschnitte.titel: A pass between north and south
abschnitte.text: A **pass** is a crossing over a mountain at the lowest possible point. The Gotthard lies in the middle of the Swiss Alps. From **Andermatt** in the canton of Uri, the road climbs to the top of the pass at just over 2,100 metres. On the other side it goes down to **Airolo** in Ticino. At the top of the pass there are small lakes, a museum and the old hospice.

The way from the north to the Gotthard leads through the narrow **Schöllenen Gorge**. There the **Reuss** roars between steep rock walls. For a long time this gorge was almost impossible to cross. In the Middle Ages only a bridge made the route possible: the **Devil's Bridge**. A well-known legend says that the devil built it and demanded as his reward the first soul to cross the bridge.

On the Ticino side, the **Tremola** winds down from the top of the pass towards Airolo. It has very many tight bends and is **cobbled** with stones. Today most cars use a newer road beside it. But the Tremola is popular with cyclists and day-trippers because it is so impressive.

Since the Middle Ages there has been a **hospice** at the top of the pass. This is a building where travellers could stay the night and warm up. In the past, **muleteers** carried goods over the pass with mules. In winter there is a great deal of snow at the top and there is a danger of **avalanches**. That is why the pass road is closed for several months every year.

Today most people travel under the Gotthard. The first **railway tunnel** between Göschenen and Airolo opened in **1882** and was then the longest tunnel in the world. Since **1980** there has been the **Gotthard Road Tunnel** for cars. In 2016 the much longer **Gotthard Base Tunnel** was added, which lies deeper in the mountain.

gewusst: At the Gotthard the paths of the water part: the Reuss flows north to the Rhine, the Ticino south to the Po.
At around 57 kilometres, the Gotthard Base Tunnel is one of the longest railway tunnels in the world.

teile.einleitung: The Linth-Limmern power stations in the canton of Glarus use water from the mountains to produce and store electricity. The heart of the scheme is a large pumped storage plant deep inside the mountain.
wichtigste: The Linth-Limmern power stations lie in the canton of Glarus.
The majority is owned by the energy company Axpo.
The Limmern pumped storage plant has a pumping and turbine output of 1,000 megawatts.
Lake Limmern serves as the lower basin.
The dam of the upper storage lake, opened in 2016, is about 1 kilometre long.
The four machine sets stand in a cavern about 600 metres deep inside the mountain.
The “Linthal 2015” extension cost about 2.1 billion francs.

abschnitte.text: The **Linth-Limmern power stations** lie at the back of the Glarus region, above Linthal in the canton of **Glarus**. They use water from the mountains to produce **electricity**. The majority of the plants belongs to the energy company **Axpo**, and a smaller part is owned by the canton of Glarus. With the major extension **“Linthal 2015”**, a new **pumped storage plant** was added. It cost about **2.1 billion francs**.

abschnitte.titel: How a pumped storage plant works
abschnitte.text: A pumped storage plant has two lakes at different heights. When there is **surplus electricity** and **electricity prices are low**, machines pump water from the **lower** to the **upper basin**. When a lot of electricity is needed later, the water flows back down and drives **turbines**. In this way the plant acts like a huge **battery**. Some of the energy is lost in the process: the **overall efficiency** of modern plants is around **75 to 80 per cent**.

The **lower basin** is **Lake Limmern**. The upper storage lake is the Muttsee. Its **dam** was opened in **2016** and is about **1 kilometre** long. It stands at about 2,500 metres above sea level. The **four machine sets** stand in a **cavern**, a huge rock hall **about 600 metres deep inside the mountain**. Together they have a pumping and turbine output of **1,000 megawatts**.

How much energy is in the water? You calculate with **potential energy**: mass times gravitational acceleration times height. **1,000 m³** of water weighs 1,000,000 kg. If this water falls **600 metres**, that gives 1,000,000 times 9.81 times 600, so about 5.9 billion joules. That is about **1.6 MWh**, or 1,600 kilowatt hours. Because the plant sends a great deal of water through the turbines, a large output is reached.

gewusst: The dam at the Muttsee is regarded as the longest dam in Switzerland.
For the construction, a large cable car was built to bring material and workers up to the height.

teile.einleitung: The Jura Water Correction is a major engineering project in the Seeland. With new canals and lower lake levels, the area between Lake Neuchâtel, Lake Biel and Lake Murten was protected from flooding.
wichtigste: The first Jura Water Correction lasted from 1868 to 1891.
The levels of the three Jura foot lakes fell by around 2.5 metres.
The engineer Richard La Nicca from the Grisons drew up the plans.
The doctor and politician Johann Rudolf Schneider campaigned for it for decades.
The cantons of Bern, Solothurn, Fribourg, Neuchâtel and Vaud took part.
The second correction lasted from 1962 to 1973.
The Port regulating weir now controls the outflow from Lake Biel.

abschnitte.text: In the past the **Seeland** was flooded again and again. The Aare and the three **Jura foot lakes**, that is, Lake Neuchâtel, Lake Biel and Lake Murten, often burst their banks. Large parts of the land were marshy, for example the **Grosses Moos**. The floods of **1831 and 1832** were especially bad. Afterwards, residents of the five affected cantons founded a **correction committee**.

The doctor and politician **Johann Rudolf Schneider** from Nidau campaigned for the project for decades. He was president of the correction committee. The plans came from the engineer **Richard La Nicca**, chief engineer of the canton of the Grisons. His plan became the basis for the work. The project was paid for by the cantons of **Bern, Solothurn, Fribourg, Neuchâtel and Vaud** together with the federal government.

The first Jura Water Correction lasted from **1868 to 1891**. The Aare was diverted into Lake Biel through a new canal. Further canals link the lakes with each other, for example the **Broye Canal** between Lake Murten and Lake Neuchâtel. The lake levels fell by around **2.5 metres**. As a result, many remains of **lake dwellings** came to light on the shores, including villages from the Bronze Age.

Even after the first correction there was still flooding. So from **1962 to 1973**, the canals were widened and deepened in the **second Jura Water Correction**. The **Port regulating weir** at the outflow of Lake Biel had already been finished in 1939. It makes it possible to control how much water flows out of the lake. On the formerly marshy land, a lot of **vegetables** are now grown.

gewusst: Because the lakes became lower, remains of villages thousands of years old were discovered on the shores.
An engineer from the Grisons planned this great project in the Seeland.

teile.einleitung: The Gotthard Base Tunnel is a railway tunnel deep beneath the Gotthard massif. At 57 kilometres it is the longest railway tunnel in the world (as of 2025).
wichtigste: Trains run through the Gotthard Base Tunnel.
At 57 km it is the longest railway tunnel in the world (as of 2025).
In the north it begins at Erstfeld in the canton of Uri.
It has two tubes for the trains.
Building it cost around 12 billion francs.
It opened in 2016 and shortens the journey to Ticino.

abschnitte.text: The **Gotthard Base Tunnel** is around **57 km** long, which makes it the **longest railway tunnel in the world** (as of 2025). It overtook the **Seikan Tunnel** in Japan. It opened in **2016**. It begins in the north at **Erstfeld** in the canton of Uri and ends in the south at Bodio in Ticino.

A **base tunnel** lies deep down at the **foot of the mountain**, not high up like older tunnels. This means the trains hardly have to climb. The highest point in the tunnel is only around **549 m above sea level**. So long, heavy freight trains can run fast, and travellers reach **Ticino** sooner.

The tunnel has **two tubes**, one for each direction. They are connected at regular intervals by cross passages. In an emergency, people can escape into the other tube. About a third and two thirds of the way along are the **multifunction stations at Sedrun and Faido**, with emergency stops.

The building work took many years and cost around **12 billion francs**. Tunnel boring machines ate their way through the hard rock. The tunnel is part of **NEAT**, the New Rail Link through the Alps. It is meant to move more goods from the road onto the **railway** and so protect the Alps.

gewusst: Inside the mountain, the rock can be over 40 °C, so the tunnel needs cooling.
Government representatives from several neighbouring countries attended the opening in 2016.

teile.einleitung: Gruyère, in German Greyerzer, is one of the best-known cheeses in Switzerland. It is named after the Gruyère region in the canton of Fribourg and is made from raw cow's milk.
wichtigste: Gruyère is made from raw cow's milk.
In German it is called “Greyerzer”.
It is a hard cheese and has almost no holes.
It matures for at least about five months in the cellar.
A wheel usually weighs between 25 and 40 kilograms.
Gruyère is an important ingredient in cheese fondue.

abschnitte.text: **Gruyère** takes its name from the region of **Gruyères** (in German Greyerz) in the canton of **Fribourg**. The pretty little town of Gruyères with its castle is also there. Today the cheese is also made in neighbouring cantons. Its name is protected as **AOP**. That means only cheese from a certain area and made according to fixed rules may carry the name.

A **cheesemaker** turns milk into cheese in the **dairy**. For Gruyère you need **raw cow's milk** from cows in the region. The milk is warmed in a big copper vat and curdled. Then the mass is broken up, put into moulds and pressed. This produces a round, flat **wheel**, which usually weighs between 25 and 40 kilograms.

Fresh cheese is still soft. So the wheels go into a **cool, damp cellar**. There they are regularly **turned** and rubbed with **salt water**. This forms a firm rind. A Gruyère matures for at least about **five months**. Many wheels mature for even longer and then taste stronger and more savoury.

Gruyère is a **hard cheese**. Its body is firm and even, and it has **almost no holes**. In this it differs from Emmental with its large holes. Young Gruyère tastes mild, while old Gruyère is savoury and sometimes slightly grainy.

Gruyère **melts well**. That is why it is in many recipes for **cheese fondue**. In the well-known “moitié-moitié” fondue, it is mixed with Vacherin Fribourgeois. It is also eaten with bread, in cheese tart or grated over a gratin. Gruyère is sold to many countries of the world.

gewusst: In Pringy near Gruyères there is a show dairy where you can watch cheese being made.
A single wheel of Gruyère needs several hundred litres of milk.

teile.einleitung: Thurgau lies in the north-east of Switzerland on Lake Constance. It is known for its many apple trees and so has the funny nickname “Mostindien” (cider India).
wichtigste: Thurgau is named after the river Thur.
In the north the canton lies on Lake Constance, with Germany on the opposite shore.
Because of the many apple trees, Thurgau is jokingly called Mostindien.
The Grand Council meets alternately in Frauenfeld and Weinfelden.
The canton is divided into 5 districts.
From 1460 to 1798 the Confederate members ruled Thurgau as a subject territory.

abschnitte.text: In Thurgau, very many **apple trees** and also pear trees grow. The fruit is used to make **Most**, that is, fruit juice, sweet or fermented. That is why the canton is jokingly called **Mostindien**. The name is a play on words: the shape of the canton on the map reminds some people of India. Besides fruit, Thurgau has a lot of farming, with vegetables, berries and dairy cows.

The **Thur** flows right across the canton. The name Thurgau means roughly “land on the Thur”. In the north the canton lies on **Lake Constance** and the Untersee. On the other side of the lake lies **Germany**. From **Romanshorn**, a car ferry crosses the lake to **Friedrichshafen**. So you can get to Germany without a long detour.

The capital of the canton is **Frauenfeld**. A special feature is the cantonal parliament, the **Grand Council**: it meets alternately in **Frauenfeld** and in **Weinfelden**. The canton is divided into **5 districts**: Arbon, Frauenfeld, Kreuzlingen, Münchwilen and Weinfelden. Kreuzlingen lies directly on the border with the German city of Konstanz.

In **1460** the Confederates conquered Thurgau. After that, several **Confederate members** ruled it jointly as a subject territory, a so-called **common lordship**. This lasted until **1798**. Thurgau has been a canton in its own right since 1803. **Napoleon III**, who later became Emperor of France, grew up at **Arenenberg Castle** on the Untersee. Today there is a museum there.

The **Ittingen Charterhouse** near Frauenfeld is a **former monastery**. For a long time, monks of the Carthusian order lived here, who keep much silence and pray alone. Today the charterhouse is a place for culture, seminars and outings. There are museums, an estate farm and a large garden.

gewusst: The Thurgau Grand Council is one of the few cantonal parliaments that meets in two different places.
Arenenberg Castle is now home to the Napoleon Museum Thurgau.

teile.einleitung: In Switzerland people are on average getting older and older. At the same time fewer children are being born. This interplay is called **demographic ageing**. It changes the world of work, pension provision and healthcare.
wichtigste: Life expectancy in Switzerland is among the highest in the world.
In 2024 it was around 86 years at birth for women and 82.5 years for men.
Around one fifth of the population is aged 65 or older.
The baby boomers, born roughly between 1946 and 1964, are now reaching retirement age.
The old-age dependency ratio compares the over 64s with the 20 to 64 year olds.
The population pyramid of Switzerland has the shape of an urn.

abschnitte.text: We speak of **demographic ageing** when the share of older people in the population grows. Two reasons are important: people live longer, and fewer children are born. **Demography** is the science that studies the population and its development. In Switzerland the **Federal Statistical Office** (FSO) collects the figures.

**Life expectancy** states how old people become on average. According to the FSO, in **2024** it was around **86 years** at birth for women and **82.5 years** for men. This puts Switzerland among the best in the world. Reasons include good nutrition, safe jobs and good medical care.

After the **Second World War** birth numbers rose strongly. The people born in the years from about **1946 to 1964** are called **baby boomers**. These large birth cohorts are now gradually reaching **retirement age**. In 2023 around **one fifth** of the population, that is about 19 to 20 per cent, were aged 65 or older. This share is still rising.

The **old-age dependency ratio** shows how many people aged 65 and over there are for every 100 people of working age, 20 to 64. If it rises, fewer people in work have to provide for more pensioners. In the past the **population pyramid** really did look like a pyramid, with many young people at the bottom. Today the base is narrow and the middle broad. This shape is called the **urn shape**.

Ageing has consequences for **pension provision**. The **AHV**, the state old-age and survivors’ insurance, is financed mainly by those who are in work today. When there are more pensioners, it needs more money. More staff are also needed in **healthcare** and in care for the elderly. How to solve these tasks is a political debate, for example about the retirement age or the financing of the AHV.

gewusst: In Switzerland women live several years longer than men on average.
The population pyramid of Switzerland is today really no longer a pyramid at all but looks more like an urn.

teile.einleitung: Household size tells you how many people live together in one household. In Switzerland, households have been getting smaller and smaller in recent decades. Today the one-person household is the most common type of household.
wichtigste: In 2022, on average around 2.2 people lived in a private household.
In 1960 it was still over three people.
Around 37 per cent of households are one-person households (2022).
Just under 30 per cent of households are couples with children.
Old people's and nursing homes count as collective households.
In large cities especially many people live alone.

abschnitte.text: A **household** is all the people who live together in one home. Statistics distinguish between **private households** and **collective households**. Collective households include, for example, **old people's and nursing homes**, boarding schools, hospitals or prisons. A **shared flat**, on the other hand, counts as a private household, even if the members are not related.

According to the **Federal Statistical Office (FSO)**, in 2022 an average of around **2.18 people** lived in a private household. In **1960** it was still over three people. The reasons are smaller families, fewer births and more people living alone. **Individualisation** also plays a part: many people want to live independently.

In 2022, around **37 per cent** of households were **one-person households** and around **33 per cent** were two-person households. Since **1970**, the number of one-person households has more than **tripled**, and today it is around 1.5 million. Because of higher **life expectancy**, many older people live alone after the death of their partner.

It is important to tell **households** and **people** apart. Around 37 per cent of the roughly 4 million households are one-person households. That is around 1.48 million people. With around 8.8 million people living in private households, only about **17 per cent** of the population live alone. Most people live with others.

In **large cities** such as Zurich, Basel or Geneva, the share of one-person households is clearly higher than in the countryside. Many young adults and older people live alone there. **Couples with children** make up just under **30 per cent** of households, and a similar number are couples without children. Smaller households need more homes overall.

gewusst: A one-person household is now more common than a household with parents and children.
Because households are getting smaller, the living space per person is rising.

teile.einleitung: In the summer of 2003, Switzerland experienced an exceptional heatwave. The Swiss heat record that still stands today was measured then. The heat had major effects on people, animals and bodies of water.
wichtigste: On 11 August 2003, 41.5 °C was measured in Grono.
This is still the official Swiss heat record today.
Grono lies in the Misox in the canton of the Grisons.
Before that, Basel held the record with 39 °C from 1952.
A blocking high brought heat for weeks.
Around 52,000 grayling died in the High Rhine.
Across Europe, several tens of thousands of people died as a result of the heat.

abschnitte.text: On **11 August 2003**, **41.5 °C** was measured in **Grono**. This was the first time over 40 °C had been reached in Switzerland. This value is still the official **national record** today. Grono lies in the **Misox** in the canton of the Grisons, on the **south side of the Alps**. The low altitude and the southern aspect favour great heat there. Before that, **Basel** held the record with **39 °C** on 2 July 1952.

abschnitte.titel: A high that would not move
abschnitte.text: The cause was a so-called **omega block**. In this, a stable **high-pressure area** sits over central Europe. On the weather map, the air flow around the high looks like the Greek letter omega. The high blocked the westerly winds for weeks. Rain and cool air could not get through, and the air kept heating up.

It was not only August that was hot. **June 2003** was around **4.7 °C** above the average for the years 1991 to 2020. That was the largest positive deviation of any month since records began in **1864**. Very little rain fell, soils dried out, and the **glaciers** lost a lot of ice.

The waters, too, became very warm. In the **High Rhine** between the Untersee and Eglisau, around **52,000 grayling** died. The **grayling** is a fish that needs cool, oxygen-rich water. In the hot summer of **2018**, the Aare became even warmer than in 2003. This again put the fish under great pressure.

Great heat is hard on the body, especially for **older people**. One study estimated around **975** additional deaths for Switzerland. Across Europe, estimates range from about **35,000 to 70,000** deaths. Since then, the authorities have issued heat warnings earlier and given tips: drink plenty, seek shade and keep homes cool.

gewusst: The 2003 heatwave is regarded as one of the deadliest natural disasters in Europe.
Basel's record from 1952 stood for over 50 years.

teile.einleitung: The Inn is a large river that rises in the Engadine in the Grisons. It flows through Austria and Germany and joins the Danube. Its water thus reaches as far as the Black Sea.
wichtigste: The Inn is about 517 kilometres long.
It rises at Lake Lunghin high above Maloja.
In Romansh it is called “En”, which is where the name Engadine comes from.
In the Upper Engadine it flows through Lake Sils, Lake Silvaplana and Lake St Moritz.
It leaves Switzerland towards Austria and flows through the Tyrol.
At Passau it joins the Danube.

abschnitte.text: The Inn rises at **Lake Lunghin** high above **Maloja** in the Upper Engadine. The mountain lake lies in a rocky landscape. Close by, at the **Lunghin Pass**, there is a special **watershed**. From here water flows in three different directions: to the North Sea, to the Mediterranean and to the Black Sea.

In Romansh the Inn is called **“En”**. This is also where the name **Engadine** comes from, that is, the valley of the Inn. In the **Upper Engadine** the Inn flows through several high-lying lakes: **Lake Sils**, **Lake Silvaplana** and **Lake St Moritz**. The well-known resort of **St Moritz** lies on Lake St Moritz. After that the Inn flows through the **Lower Engadine** with places such as Zernez and Scuol.

In the Lower Engadine the Inn leaves Switzerland. Shortly after the border it flows through the narrow pass of **Finstermünz**. There the **Upper Inn Valley** begins in **Tyrol**. The Tyrolean capital **Innsbruck** has the river in its name. Innsbruck means “bridge over the Inn”.

abschnitte.titel: Into the Danube and the Black Sea
abschnitte.text: The Inn is about **517 kilometres** long. Most of it lies in Austria and Germany. In the German city of **Passau** it joins the **Danube**. The Danube flows on eastwards through many countries. Finally its water reaches the **Black Sea**. The Inn is the only large Swiss river whose water flows there.

gewusst: At Passau the Inn often carries more water than the Danube itself at the confluence.
On the lakes of the Upper Engadine, people often sail and windsurf, because a wind called the Maloja wind blows there regularly.

teile.einleitung: The Leventina is a long valley in the north of the canton of Ticino. The Ticino river flows through it from the Gotthard down to Biasca, and for centuries the most important route over the Alps to the south has run here.
wichtigste: The Leventina is the valley of the Ticino.
It stretches from Airolo at the foot of the Gotthard Pass to Biasca.
The main town of the Leventina district is Faido.
Until 1798 the valley was a subject territory of the canton of Uri.
In 1755 an uprising against the bailiffs was put down.
The old Gotthard railway overcomes the steep steps with spiral tunnels.
At Bodio lies the south portal of the Gotthard Base Tunnel.

abschnitte.text: The Leventina begins at **Airolo**, just below the Gotthard Pass. From there the **Ticino** flows down the valley to the south east. At **Biasca**, the Brenno flows in from the Blenio Valley, and here the Leventina ends. The valley has several steps: calm, broader stretches alternate with narrow gorges. In the Leventina people speak Italian.

The main town is **Faido**. It was already the centre of the valley earlier, even when the people of Uri ruled here. Today the Leventina forms a **district** of its own in the canton of Ticino. Other places are Airolo, Giornico and Bodio. Many old stone houses and churches recall the long history.

In the Middle Ages, **Uri** wanted to control the route over the Gotthard. With its victory in the **Battle of Giornico** in 1478, Uri secured the valley. The Leventina became a **subject territory**, run by bailiffs. In 1755 the people of the Leventina rose up against this rule. The **Leventina uprising** was put down, and the leaders were executed in Faido. Only with the end of the Old Confederation in 1798 was the time of subjection over.

The old **Gotthard railway** runs through the whole Leventina. At the gorges of **Piottino** and **Biaschina** the valley is very steep. So that the trains do not have to climb too steeply, the railway gains height in circular **spiral tunnels**. In the tunnel the train goes once round in a circle and comes out higher up. For travellers it is a special experience, because you see the same church several times from different sides.

Since 2016 there has been the **Gotthard Base Tunnel**. It is 57 kilometres long and runs from Erstfeld in the canton of Uri to **Bodio** in the Leventina. Many trains now travel deep under the mountain and reach the south much faster. The A2 motorway also runs through the Leventina, from the Gotthard Road Tunnel at Airolo to Biasca.

gewusst: In the spiral tunnels of the Leventina you see the same church several times on the train, because the railway winds its way up in loops.
The Gotthard Base Tunnel, with its south portal at Bodio, is the longest railway tunnel in the world.

teile.einleitung: The higher you climb into the mountains, the colder it gets. That is why different plants grow at different heights. These zones are called altitudinal zones. In the Swiss Alps, five of them are distinguished.
wichtigste: The lowest zone is the colline zone, with vineyards and orchards.
Above it lies the montane zone with beech, fir and spruce forests.
In the subalpine zone, larches and Swiss stone pines grow up to the tree line.
The tree line lies roughly between 1,800 and 2,300 metres.
Above the tree line comes the alpine zone with alpine pastures.
At the very top lies the nival zone with rock, snow and ice.

abschnitte.text: The **colline zone** is the **hill zone** at low altitudes. The name comes from the Latin word for hill. It is warm enough there for **vines**, **fruit** and **arable farming**. Most of the towns and villages of Switzerland lie in this zone. Naturally, deciduous forests grow there, for example with oaks and beeches.

Above the hill zone begins the **montane zone**, the **mountain forest zone**. On the north side of the Alps, **beech and fir forests** often grow there, with many spruces higher up. The **beech** is a typical deciduous tree of this zone. On the south side of the Alps, by contrast, the **sweet chestnut** is common. Many mountain villages lie in this zone.

abschnitte.titel: Subalpine zone and the tree line
abschnitte.text: In the **subalpine zone** the forest becomes more open. Here mainly **larches** and **Swiss stone pines** grow. They cope very well with cold and short summers and often form the uppermost forest. The **tree line** in the Swiss Alps lies roughly between **1,800 and 2,300 metres**. At the northern edge of the Alps it is lower, and in the drier inner Alps it is higher.

Above the tree line it is too cold for trees. In the **alpine zone** there are **alpine pastures** with grasses, alpine flowers and low shrubs such as the **alpenrose**. In early summer, farmers drive their cows up to the **alp** in the **alpine ascent**. In autumn they return to the valley in the **alpine descent**.

The uppermost zone is the **nival zone**. The name comes from the Latin word for snow. It lies above the **snow line** and consists of rock, snow and ice. Plants only grow there here and there in cracks in the rock, for example the **glacier crowfoot**. On the warmer **south side of the Alps**, all the altitudinal zones usually lie somewhat higher than on the north side.

gewusst: The glacier crowfoot is one of the flowering plants that grow highest in the Alps.
For every 100 metres of height, it gets on average about half a degree colder.

teile.einleitung: Basel-Stadt is the smallest canton in Switzerland. It lies on the Rhine on the border with Germany and France and is known for its university, its museums and the Basel Carnival.
wichtigste: Only three municipalities belong to the canton: Basel, Riehen and Bettingen.
The Rhine divides Basel into Grossbasel and Kleinbasel.
The University of Basel was founded in 1460 and is the oldest in Switzerland.
The town hall on the Marktplatz is painted bright red.
Basel Minster is built of red sandstone.
Since 2017 the Basel Carnival has been part of UNESCO's intangible cultural heritage.
Basler Läckerli are a well-known speciality.

abschnitte.text: The **Rhine** flows right through Basel. It divides the city into **Grossbasel** and **Kleinbasel**, and several bridges cross the river. There are also **ferries** without engines. They hang from a cable above the river, and the **current** pushes them from one bank to the other. Only three municipalities belong to the canton: the city of **Basel** and **Riehen** and **Bettingen**.

High above the Rhine stands **Basel Minster**. It is built of **red sandstone** and so glows reddish. The scholar **Erasmus of Rotterdam**, who lived in Basel and died in 1536, is buried in the Minster. On the Marktplatz stands the **town hall**, painted bright red. It is one of the best-known buildings in the city.

The **University of Basel** was founded in **1460**. It is the oldest university in Switzerland. A landmark of Basel is the **basilisk**, a mythical creature, half cockerel and half dragon. You can see it on many fountains in the city. Basel also has very many **museums**, for example for art, history and toys.

The **Basel Carnival** begins with the **Morgenstreich** at four o'clock in the morning, when all the lights in the old town go out. Then **cliques** with lanterns, piccolos and drums march through the lanes. In **2017**, the Basel Carnival was added to the intangible cultural heritage of **UNESCO**. A well-known speciality is the **Läckerli**, small hard gingerbreads with honey and spices.

gewusst: In Basel you can cross the Rhine on a ferry that is driven only by the current.
Near Basel, Switzerland, Germany and France meet. This spot is called the Dreiländereck (“tri-country corner”).

teile.einleitung: The Chapel Bridge in Lucerne is a covered wooden bridge over the Reuss. It is the best-known landmark of the city and one of the oldest wooden bridges in Europe.
wichtigste: The Chapel Bridge is built mainly of wood.
It was built in the 14th century.
Its name comes from the nearby St Peter's Chapel.
Under the roof hang triangular painted panels.
In 1993 the bridge burned down for the most part.
Next to the bridge stands the octagonal Water Tower.
Today only pedestrians may cross the bridge.

abschnitte.text: The **Chapel Bridge** crosses the **Reuss** at an angle in Lucerne, where the river flows out of Lake Lucerne. It is about 200 metres long and built mainly of **wood**. A roof protects it from rain and snow, which is why it is called a **covered bridge**. It was built in the **14th century**. Today only **pedestrians** may cross it.

The bridge is named after **St Peter's Chapel**, a small church on the bank nearby. In the past the bridge was part of the **town fortifications** of Lucerne. It protected the city against attacks from the lake. Only later did it become mainly a way to get comfortably from one bank to the other.

Up under the roof hang **painted panels**. They are **triangular** because they fit exactly into the shape of the gable. The pictures were painted in the 17th century. They show events from the history of Lucerne and Switzerland, as well as scenes from the lives of the city's patron saints. In this way the bridge told people history in pictures.

In August **1993** a **fire** broke out on the bridge. Large parts of the Chapel Bridge burned down, and many of the old pictures were destroyed. The city quickly rebuilt the bridge, and by 1994 people could cross it again. Some of the rescued pictures hang in their old places again, and on others you can still see the marks of the fire.

In the middle of the river next to the bridge stands the **Water Tower**. It is **octagonal** and built of stone. The tower is older than the bridge. Over time it served as a watchtower, a prison, an archive and a treasury. Together, the Chapel Bridge and the Water Tower make one of the best-known photo subjects in Switzerland.

gewusst: The Chapel Bridge is regarded as one of the oldest covered wooden bridges in Europe.
After the fire of 1993 the bridge was rebuilt in less than a year.

teile.einleitung: French is one of the four national languages of Switzerland. It is spoken mainly in the west, in the Romandie, and has some words of its own there.
wichtigste: French is the second largest national language of Switzerland.
The French-speaking part of Switzerland is called the Romandie, its inhabitants Romands.
In the Romandie people say septante for 70 and nonante for 90.
In Vaud people say huitante for 80.
Many Romands call lunch dîner and the evening meal souper.
Lake Geneva is mostly called Lac Léman in French.

abschnitte.text: After German, French is the **second largest national language** of Switzerland. It is spoken in the **Romandie** in the west. Entirely French-speaking are the cantons of **Geneva**, **Vaud**, **Neuchâtel** and **Jura**. In **Fribourg**, in the **Valais** and in **Bern** people speak German and French.

In France people say “soixante-dix” for 70, that is, sixty plus ten. In the Romandie people say more simply **septante**. For 90 they say **nonante** instead of “quatre-vingt-dix”. In **Vaud**, in Fribourg and in the Valais people often say **huitante** for 80. In Belgium too people say septante and nonante.

There are differences with meals too. Many Romands call breakfast **déjeuner**, lunch **dîner** and the evening meal **souper**. In France, by contrast, lunch is mostly called “déjeuner” and the evening meal “dîner”. On visits this can lead to funny misunderstandings.

**Lake Geneva** is mostly called **Lac Léman** in French. Some words in the Romandie come from German, for example “poutzer” for putzen, to clean. Such special features are called **Helvetisms**. They show how the languages in Switzerland influence one another.

gewusst: In the past various dialects were spoken in the Romandie, called Franco-Provençal, which has almost disappeared today.
In Biel/Bienne German and French have equal status, and the street signs are bilingual.

teile.einleitung: The Grisons is the largest canton in Switzerland. It lies in the south-east, has very many valleys and mountains and is the only canton with three official languages: German, Romansh and Italian. The capital is Chur.
wichtigste: The Grisons borders three countries: Italy, Austria and Liechtenstein.
The coat of arms includes a black ibex, among other things.
The red trains of the Rhaetian Railway run over many bridges and through many tunnels.
The Landwasser Viaduct near Filisur is around 65 metres high.
The San Bernardino links the Grisons with Ticino.
Capuns, Bündnerfleisch and Nusstorte are specialities of the Grisons.
The story of Heidi is set above Maienfeld.

abschnitte.text: By area, the Grisons is the **largest canton** in Switzerland. It borders **Italy**, **Austria** and **Liechtenstein**, and the borders mostly run through high mountains. Here **German**, **Romansh** and **Italian** are spoken. The **coat of arms of the Grisons** has three parts, one of which shows a black **ibex**. The **Swiss National Park**, the only national park in Switzerland, also lies in the Grisons.

The **Rhaetian Railway**, with its red trains, runs through many valleys of the canton. The **Albula** and **Bernina lines** are UNESCO World Heritage. Famous is the **Landwasser Viaduct** near Filisur. The bridge is around **65 metres** high and leads straight into a tunnel in the rock face. On such routes the trains overcome great differences in height.

Over the **San Bernardino Pass** and through the tunnel beneath it runs the **A13** motorway from Chur to Bellinzona in **Ticino**. Near Thusis lies the **Viamala**, a narrow and deep gorge of the **Hinterrhein**. In the past the way through it was very dangerous, hence the name, which means “bad way”. The Grisons has many more passes, for example the Julier and the Albula.

For **Capuns**, a dough with small pieces of meat is wrapped in **chard leaves** and cooked in milk and stock. **Bündnerfleisch** is beef that is salted and **air-dried** for weeks in the dry mountain air. The **Bündner Nusstorte** is filled with walnuts and caramel. Johanna Spyri had her character **Heidi** live on an alp above **Maienfeld**. That is why the area is now also called **Heidiland**.

gewusst: The Grisons is the only canton in Switzerland with three official languages.
The Swiss National Park in the Engadine was founded in 1914 and is one of the oldest in Europe.

teile.einleitung: In Bellinzona, the main town of the canton of Ticino, stand three mighty castles. Together with long walls they used to block the valley. Today they belong to the **UNESCO World Heritage** and are a popular destination for outings.
wichtigste: In Bellinzona stand three castles: Castelgrande, Montebello and Sasso Corbaro.
Castelgrande is the largest castle and stands on a rocky hill in the middle of the city.
Sasso Corbaro lies highest, Montebello lies in between.
The castles and walls blocked the way through the valley to the Alpine passes.
